results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 53 outline summaries match the controlling idea of the aligned spec paragraph, in spec order (p01-p53, with the architecture section's declared order p19, p20, p24, p25, p21, p22, p23, p26, p27, p28); the five intro callouts are outside the spec's paragraph list.
Introduction para 3 (marked two_ideas): place in Part VIII, the three owned terms and the hand-offs form one context idea, exactly as p03's controlling idea declares; not two arguments.

In Practice para 9 (marked two_ideas): the permanent-federation classification and its corollary (most separable, neutrality and separability need the same architecture) are one idea as p37 declares it; the loosely tied real-estate evidence sentence is judged under evidence_is_explained and flow_is_followable.
Every unit ties to a supporting claim S1-S5 or to the scene/judging function the spec gives it; the Tradeyard/Motorvane paragraph ties to S1 (merge brands declined).

All tables, Figures 1-6 and the quotations (Immowelt/Ultimmo, Adevinta, Kleinanzeigen, OLX, Worldline, Google, mobile.de, Bundeskartellamt) are framed or followed by a sentence saying what they show, except the item failed separately.

results.quote: The real-estate evidence points the same way: a portal that owns the software agents use to originate listings holds a strong position, and the agencies and competition authorities know it
results.finding: The case-aviv evidence is not followed by what it shows for the paragraph's claim: it is about a portal's market power, and the draft never says how that supports 'neutrality and separability require the same architecture' (e.g. agencies and regulators distrust a portal-owned CRM, so it must stay visibly separate).

Every declared transition_in (introduction p02-p04, each section's opening, each paragraph boundary and the conclusion's p52/p53) is expressed at its boundary and picks up the declared known information; section-opening definitions in Concepts lean on their subheadings and on p10's 'four concepts' announcement, which suffices.

Both readers describe the organising principle as problem (scene) -> concepts -> method -> worked case -> generalisation (trade-offs, verticals, failure modes) -> decisions, matching the declared problem_solution with prerequisite_order and grouping; neither marks any section's position unclear. Names from earlier chapters both readers queried (Hearthly, Common Ground, Veldmark ID, Ingrid's role, tenant code) are on audience.already_knows and are not counted.

results.quote: The review applied the same choice of option inside the group, to the one place where a synergy case might have proposed merging two of Veldmark's own brands. That overlap needed a portfolio decision, not a platform one.
results.finding: Reader A item 12: 'This paragraph was the hardest to follow... The paragraph also circles: a choice of option, then "a portfolio decision, not a platform one", then a decision already made elsewhere and kept. On a first read I could not tell what the review actually decided.' The prose does not state the decision (merge brands declined, existing split kept) before circling through its framings. Both readers also suggest relocating the paragraph; that is an order question for the author, but the shared difficulty is fixable in the prose.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 9 ('It felt like a detour... ends by keeping a decision that was already recorded, not by choosing an integration option')

results.quote: The two sentences that justify an acquisition compete hardest when the product moves first
results.finding: Reader A item 13: 'In the opening it was liquidity and platform change, the subjects of the two sentences, that compete for months, teams and risk budget, not the sentences themselves. The compressed phrasing made me go back and check.'
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 14 ('Saying that the sentences themselves compete is a slightly odd compression')

results.finding: 'Carve-out' is on audience.does_not_know (deal vocabulary) and the draft never defines a carve-out deal; the synergy table's 'carving the business out again if it is sold' describes a later sale, not an acquisition carved out of a seller, so the stage-0 condition is opaque to this reader.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader A, item 14 ('"carve-out" ... without a gloss. Transitional services are explained earlier, in the Divest row, but carve-out is not')

results.finding: The introduction opens with a direct statement of the two-sentence deal rationale and its tension, then the public record, the chapter's place and terms, and a roadmap; none of the five weak patterns.
The conclusion does not open with 'in conclusion', adds no new subtopic or body evidence, and does more than rephrase the thesis.

p52 joins the parts into one mechanism no section states (sequence decides which synergies arrive, gates when, ledger prices each delay) and gives the so-what: the Chief Architect can tell the owner where the synergies are before being asked.

p52 returns to the opening's two sentences that justify an acquisition and to the owner's question of where the synergies are (Henrik de Boer's forwarded question); the compressed wording of the callback is failed separately under flow_is_followable.

The cold reader predicted, in order, the Veldmark question on Casavista and Keybridge, the options and three terms, the gated bottom-up sequence and separate brand workstream, the review with ledger and one internal overlap, and the closing sections; evidence from eBay, AVIV, OLX, Adevinta and the fictional Veldmark case; a declarative practitioner tone. This matches AC-2's expected and every roadmap promise.

The AC-1 reader names the inverted sequence (trust and identity before product, product last with its own investment case), migrating to the group target rather than a sibling due for replacement, liquidity gates instead of dates, a separate brand workstream with the 3% organic-sessions rule, a ledger with traffic loss, double running and separation cost, and a named, DPO-signed permission for the CRM data line that the neutrality situation may forbid. All elements of the expected answer are present.
